name: Erigeron

project_scope.source_pool_synonym: Conyza canadensis maps to Erigeron canadensis, no duplicate species card
project_scope.science_status: Native-target-county certification is not settled by this genus reconciliation; retain each species' own unresolved/previous statuses.
project_scope.lesson_scope: Five of five canonical Erigeron cards, 16 local source-credited exact-species photos, 2 extra horseweed licensed early-flower remote references, new USGS PUBLIC DOMAIN Philadelphia upper-leaf photographic proof, CC0 Geiser's pressed root-zone source reuse. Current genus lesson visually usable for crew, scientific photo hold remains for crown comparison and fully paired leafbase macro. E. annuus / tenuis / tenellus remain comparison-only.

look_here_first: FIVE-SPECIES FIELD KEY. Tiny inconspicuously rayed terminal HEADS on a tall narrow-leaved stalk → E. canadensis (horseweed). Showy daisy rays? Check the BASE: slender annual taproot → E. geiseri; mature woody perennial crown → E. modestus. For leafy many-headed fleabanes check UPPER LEAF BASE: normally nonclasping, often ~50–100 rays → E. strigosus; clasping/auriculate, often ~150–250+ rays → E. philadelphicus. Use multiple characters. Do not identify from flower color alone.
shared_traits: Asteraceae composite capitula with many minute florets
Alternate leaves on horseweed (other Erigeron leaf architecture varies)
Wind dispersed one-seeded cypsela with white pappus hairs
Flowering head size and ray length more discriminating than common name

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Annual or winter annual; often one erect main stalk 50–200 cm, branches mainly at TOP
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: Many Erigeron spp. have smaller branched stems arising from basal rosette, but can overlap
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Full rooted plant with lower stem and flowering arrangement

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Numerous tiny heads with INVOLUCRES about 3–4 mm LONG; short pale rays ~0.5–1 mm can be inconspicuous. Avoid treating mature white seed fluff as fresh rays.
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: E. strigosus usually has showy white rays (~50–100 at ~4–6 mm). E. philadelphicus has many more finer rays (~150–250+). Numbers overlap in field quality; measure a fresh head and check leaves/hairs.
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Fresh OPEN flowering head front + side, millimeter ruler; a fruit pappus picture does not prove ray length.

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Narrow sessile linear-oblanceolate stem leaves, frequently shallowly toothed low down
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: E. strigosus upper narrow leaves usually do NOT clasp; lower leaves often persist and may be entire or toothed. E. philadelphicus upper leaves often clasp; E. annuus often coarser leaves and spreading hairs.
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Leaf at lower, middle, upper nodes with scale

comparison_matrix.horseweed: Many tiny cypselae with white pappus 2–3 mm
comparison_matrix.fleabanes: Also pappus fruit — not independently diagnostic
comparison_matrix.photo_need: Single head and seed after flowering

lookalike_warnings: Conyza canadensis is an older/alternative genus combination, not a second horseweed species.
Conyza bonariensis and C. sumatrensis may appear as lookalikes in disturbed plants, but detailed head/hair characters needed; don't claim all are local or native.

All five species E. canadensis, geiseri, modestus, philadelphicus and strigosus are installed in the learner as separate canonical cards; the latter two currently have ONE provisional exact-species photo each, NOT fully finished photo galleries. Never treat them as uninstalled or duplicate a prior card.
Horseweed tiny flowers are not goldenrod: goldenrod has YELLOW composite heads with much more showy yellow rays.

part_examples.title: 1 · Begin with the winter rosette
part_examples.look_for: The larger notched/toothed-leaved rosette is horseweed. A SMALL separate Draba verna rosette is also in the frame; do not label both species as horseweed.
part_examples.why_it_matters: A rosette-only ID should remain provisional; return to the same plant when it bolts.

part_examples.title: 2 · Trace the upright leafy stem
part_examples.look_for: Follow the tall single stem, alternate narrow leaves and many upward branches ending in tiny pale heads.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Shows horseweed's mature architecture and how it differs from daisy-like fleabanes.

part_examples.title: 3 · Fruiting pappus macro (NOT open ray florets)
part_examples.role: Fruiting head: pappus and spent receptacle
part_examples.look_for: At center, a spent head; surrounding fine white filaments are PAPPUS attached to fruits. This specific photo does not show the short pale rays of an actively blooming horseweed head.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Pappus bristles are not petals; use a fresh flowering photo for ray-floret teaching.

part_examples.title: 4 · Find the feathery pappus
part_examples.look_for: Later wispy fruiting structure with pappus; broad green foreground blade is not confidently attributable to the photographed horseweed.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Connects flowers to dispersal and highlights a shared composite fruit character.

part_examples.title: 5 · NEED PHOTO — actual horseweed OPEN flowers vs showy fleabane
part_examples.look_for: Bring same-scale photos with a ruler: horseweed with green involucre ~3–4 mm LONG and very short fresh whitish marginal rays, versus E. strigosus or E. philadelphicus with obviously longer daisy-like rays.
part_examples.why_it_matters: A direct visual pair teaches how ray length and head architecture separate common confusions without mistaking flower color for a full ID.

part_examples.title: 6 · Prairie fleabane's true white rays
part_examples.look_for: White rays around yellow disc on a slender flowering shoot (dog in background); strong composite-head clue but NOT sufficient for species alone.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Contrasts with the tiny, hard-to-see rays of horseweed. Stem hair/leaf-base macros missing.

part_examples.title: 7 · Philadelphia fleabane's many rays
part_examples.look_for: Many slender pale rays around yellow discs; do NOT claim photo proves clasping upper leaves.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Crew comparison: true tie-breaker involves leaf attachment and stem hairs as well as head measurements.

part_examples.title: 8 · Philadelphia fleabane: upper leaf-base junction
part_examples.role: linked vegetative photo; potential auriculate clasp
part_examples.look_for: Observe where upper alternate leaf joins stem. FNA identifies clasping auricles, but image angle leaves full wrap uncertain.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Separates typical philadelphicus from usually nonclasping strigosus; need side macro.

part_examples.title: 9 · Philadelphia fleabane: many fine pink-white rays
part_examples.look_for: Numerous very narrow rays around yellow tubular disc florets and an unopened pink head; not pappus-stage hair.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Contrasts especially with horseweed's extremely short rays.

part_examples.title: 10 · Horseweed emerging white ray florets, 6-mm reference
part_examples.look_for: Short white emerging ray florets above narrow green phyllaries; separate 6-mm bar. The central yellow disc is not yet exposed and bristles are NOT mature seed pappus.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Separates an unopened green composite head, early flower rays and later floating seed hairs on real photos, not guesses.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: HORSEWEED = tiny heads (emerging rays vs mature fluff). PRAIRIE vs PHILADELPHIA = UPPER LEAF BASE: typically NONCLASPING vs CLASPING (now photographed). GEISER'S vs PLAINS = ANNUAL SLENDER ROOT vs WOODY PERENNIAL CROWN (needs a real field root view). If decisive part hidden, STOP at Erigeron sp.

genus_diagnostics.flower_heads: All Erigeron members are composite-family plants bearing capitula (flower heads with many little florets), not single big flowers. HORSEWEED has extremely small heads with barely visible short rays; many other fleabanes have obvious longer daisy-like rays. Don't generalize horseweed's almost rayless look to the whole genus.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Often alternate simple foliage, but leaf shape varies greatly among fleabanes. Horseweed forms a rosette first, then alternate narrow stem leaves. Study BOTH seasons before identifying the species.
genus_diagnostics.stem: In horseweed a single upright, leafy main stem branches into a broad narrow-headed terminal panicle. Other Erigeron may be much shorter or hold one/several showier heads. Whole-plant architecture is important but not definitive alone.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Compare head size, number, rays and the panicle shape. Horseweed has scores to hundreds of heads just a few millimeters across; many fleabanes have larger radiate heads that resemble tiny daisies.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Mature Erigeron cypselae generally have a pappus aiding wind dispersal. The horseweed photograph shows fluffy mature heads; a single dry cypsela and attachment of bristles needs a millimeter-scale macro.

order: Whole rooted plant and basal crown
Head diameter, rays and phyllary profile at matched scale
Stem and leaf hairs under magnification
overlap_cautions: Head sizes and ray characters can overlap between showy fleabanes; don't force identification from a single measurement.
A rosette alone is insufficient to confirm horseweed.
The two source-pool candidates are not canonical learner cards; installer lane must resolve accepted identity and eligibility.

rows: Erigeron canadensis
Annual/winter annual; rosette then tall erect stem
Numerous tiny heads ~3–4 mm; rays inconspicuous
Narrow alternate stem leaves; upper branching
Good mature architecture; rosette alone uncertain
Erigeron geiseri
Annual with slender taproot (NOT a perennial woody crown)
Showy fleabane rays ~3–6 mm, ~44–70 rays; measure flowering head
Lower stem hairs spreading/deflexed, upper hairs more appressed; compare to E. modestus
Existing species card has morphological diagnosis; not a county-range PASS
Erigeron modestus
Perennial; inspect intact root crown
Showy fleabane-like rays; measurements may overlap E. geiseri
Compare basal leaves, hair distribution and involucre
Needs paired voucher-confirmed specimens
Erigeron strigosus
Annual / biennial / short-lived perennial, sometimes rhizomatous by variety; basal leaves often persist
Many showy white rays (FNA 50–100), ~4–6 mm; loose branched clusters
Narrow, progressively reduced upper leaves usually nonclasping; margins entire OR toothed; mostly appressed/ascending hairs
Key-based field lesson; root, leaf node and stem hairs NOT photo-proven in current one-photo source
Erigeron philadelphicus
Annual, biennial or short-lived perennial, fibrous rooted
FNA 150–250(–400) slender white/pink rays ~5–10 mm; involucre 4–6 × 6–15 mm
Upper stem leaves CLASP/auriculate-clasp; lower foliage often crenate/toothed; proximal stems often spreading-hairy
Flower & leaves shown across linked photo roles, but complete clasping-ear, hairs and cypsela macros not yet proven

comparison_cards.title: Horseweed versus showy fleabanes
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Look at a FRESH head: horseweed has scores of very tiny heads on a tall leafy axis; the measured 6-mm licensed macro actually shows short ray tips and green phyllaries. Contrast late ripe pappus, which is fruit, NOT flowers. Showy fleabanes have clearly larger rays.

comparison_cards.title: Geiser's versus plains fleabane

Support with stem hairs, basal habit and correctly measured ray counts.
